# Where we are

## Recap

Three classes, three arguments that the physical story leaves something out.

- Russell: what you're immediately aware of isn't the table.
- Nagel: no amount of bat neuroscience tells you what it's like to be one.
- Jackson: Mary knew all the physics and still learned something.

. . .

Each of them says something is missing. None of them says what the missing thing *is*.

## Today

Today we meet the view with the most direct answer to that question.

. . .

The missing thing is missing because minds aren't physical things at all.

# The flying man

## Back to Ibn Sīnā

## The case

:::: {.callout-note title="Adamson"}
Imagine, he says, that a person is created by God in mid-air, in good condition but with his sight veiled and his limbs outstretched so that he is touching nothing, not even his own body. This person has no memories, having only just been created.
::::

## What it's meant to show

:::: {.callout-note title="Adamson"}
The flying man is aware of himself; he knows that he exists. But he is not aware of his body; he doesn't know that his body exists.
::::

. . .

So there is something he knows about himself that he doesn't know about his body. And if that's right, he isn't his body.

## Note what isn't argued for

:::: {.callout-note title="Adamson"}
Avicenna does not attempt to *argue* that the flying man would know that he exists. Rather, he takes it as obvious.
::::

. . .

Whether that's a weakness depends on whether you agree. Most people, asked, do.

## iClicker QUIZ

In Adamson's telling, which of these is **not** part of the flying man's situation?

A.  His sight is veiled
B.  His limbs are held apart so he touches nothing, not even himself
C.  He has just been created, and has no memories
D.  He has been stripped of his capacity to reason

# The trouble with the argument

## One objection, used twice

Adamson raises the problem himself, and it's worth getting clear on, because it comes back in ten minutes against a much more famous argument.

:::: {.callout-note title="Adamson"}
One can be conscious of a thing without being conscious of everything about it.
::::

## Why that bites

I know the person at the front of this room is your lecturer. I might not know he's the one who left the lights on in Angell Hall last night.

. . .

It doesn't follow that your lecturer isn't that person.

. . .

Knowing about a thing under one description and not another tells you about descriptions. It doesn't by itself tell you there are two things.

## What's left

Adamson thinks something survives anyway.

:::: {.callout-note title="Adamson"}
All Avicenna has really done is to throw down a challenge to his materialist opponents: show me how a body could be aware of itself without using sensation to do so.
::::

. . .

A challenge is less than a proof. It is not nothing.

# Descartes

## Six hundred years later

Descartes runs an argument with the same shape, and it is the most discussed argument in the history of the subject.

By the end of the *Meditations* he thinks he has established two things he can be certain of: that he exists as a thinking thing, and that God exists and is no deceiver.

. . .

The second lets him trust whatever he perceives **clearly and distinctly**.

## The real distinction

1. I clearly and distinctly understand my mind as a thinking, non-extended thing.
2. I clearly and distinctly understand my body as an extended, non-thinking thing.
3. Clear and distinct perception can be trusted.
4. So the two can be separated, at least by God.

. . .

5. So my mind is really distinct from my body, and can exist without it.

## The same objection, again

Line 4 is where the weight sits. Understanding A without understanding B is a fact about your understanding.

. . .

Getting from there to *A and B can come apart* needs the step that whatever you can clearly and distinctly conceive is possible.

. . .

That is exactly the move we have just seen fail for the flying man. Descartes needs God to make it work, which tells you how much work it is doing.

## Not a sailor in a ship

One thing Descartes is careful to deny. He is not saying you merely pilot your body from inside it.

The union is tighter than that: you don't *observe* that your body is damaged, you feel pain.

. . .

Hold on to that, because it is about to cost him.

# Varieties of dualism

## Substance dualism

:::: {.callout-note title="Berger"}
Substance dualism proposes that minds are substances that think, feel, and experience, but do not take up space and could exist without bodies.
::::

A substance is something that can exist on its own. This is the view Descartes and Ibn Sīnā are arguing for.

## Property dualism

:::: {.callout-note title="Berger"}
Property dualism holds that creatures may have distinct mental and physical properties, although they perhaps cannot have mental features without also having physical ones.
::::

. . .

There is one kind of stuff. It has two kinds of feature, and one of them isn't physical.

## Which one do you get?

Nagel and Jackson, if they work, get you property dualism. Something about experience isn't captured physically.

. . .

They don't get you a separable soul. For that you need the flying man or the real distinction, and those are the two arguments we have just watched struggle.

# Thought and feeling, again

## The distinction from Day 11

Thinking
:    Whatever we do with observations of the world and combinations of them. Reasoning, planning, inferring.

Consciousness
:    There being something it is like, for the thing itself.

. . .

I said these were two concepts, not one, and that any link between them needs an argument. Here's the argument, and here's who makes it.

## The grid

|                       | **Conscious**        | **Not conscious** |
|-----------------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| **Thinks**            | you, right now       | ?                 |
| **Doesn't think**     | ?                    | a rock            |

. . .

Descartes fills in the two corners and leaves the other two empty. Everything that thinks feels, and everything that feels thinks.

## Why he's entitled to that

It isn't stubbornness. It follows from the view.

If thought and consciousness are both modes of one mental substance, then whatever has either has both. Soul, or no soul.

. . .

Which means the diagonal is a consequence of **substance** dualism in particular. Give up the substance and you have given up the reason for it.

## A quick question (POLL)

**Which of the two empty boxes is really empty?**

A.  Thinks but isn't conscious — nothing could be like that
B.  Conscious but doesn't think — nothing could be like that
C.  Both. Nothing occupies either
D.  Neither. Both have occupants

. . .

You have met a candidate for one of them already, on Thursday.

## The occupants

**Thinks, not conscious.** The zombie from last week is exactly this cell. So, less exotically, is blindsight, and so is all the processing below awareness we met back on Days 3 and 6.

. . .

**Conscious, doesn't think.** A creature that feels pain and fear and nothing much else. Most people are readier to grant this one than to say what the cut-off is.

## The irony

Almost nobody in this room is a substance dualist.

. . .

But the slide from *it thinks* to *it feels*, and back, is everywhere — not least in what people say about machines.

. . .

That slide is a Cartesian conclusion. If you've dropped the Cartesian premise, you need some other reason for it, and there isn't an obvious one lying around.

## Animals

Descartes is often reported as holding that animals feel nothing at all, because feeling would require a soul and he denied them one.

. . .

Whether that's a fair reading of him has been argued about for fifty years, so treat the slogan with care.^[John Cottingham, "'A Brute to the Brutes?': Descartes' Treatment of Animals," *Philosophy* 53 (1978).]

. . .

What isn't in doubt is the pressure. Line up all three distinctions and the yelping dog has nothing going on. That is a cost, and we'll meet the bill again in the ethics unit.
